stimuli.title: Passage 1: Flow through a narrowed artery
stimuli.text:
A team of researchers built a bench model of a carotid artery partly blocked by plaque. They treated blood as an incompressible fluid of density 1,060 kg/m³ flowing steadily through a rigid horizontal tube. Upstream of the plaque the tube has a radius of 4.0 mm and the mean flow speed is 0.30 m/s. Over a short segment the plaque narrows the radius to 2.0 mm.

For an ideal fluid, the continuity equation (A1v1 = A2v2) and Bernoulli's equation (P + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant along a streamline) describe the flow. Real blood is viscous, and in long vessels the researchers used Poiseuille's law instead:

Q = πΔP r⁴ / (8ηL)

where Q is the volume flow rate, ΔP the pressure difference along a vessel of length L and radius r, and η the viscosity of the fluid. The team noted that a short stenosis mainly raises the local speed, while narrowing along a long vessel mainly raises resistance.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: The bicarbonate buffer
stimuli.text:
Most of the carbon dioxide made by tissues is carried in blood as bicarbonate:

CO2(aq) + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H⁺ + HCO3⁻

Red blood cells contain carbonic anhydrase, which speeds the first step. Because H2CO3 is present only in tiny amounts, clinicians treat dissolved CO2 as the acid and use an apparent pKa of 6.1:

pH = 6.1 + log([HCO3⁻] / [CO2])

Dissolved CO2 (in mM) equals 0.03 times the arterial partial pressure of CO2 (PaCO2, in mmHg). The lungs can change PaCO2 within minutes; the kidneys adjust bicarbonate over hours to days. Arterial values for four hypothetical patients are shown below.

| Patient | PaCO2 (mmHg) | HCO3⁻ (mM) |
|---|---|---|
| W | 40 | 24 |
| X | 80 | 24 |
| Y | 40 | 12 |
| Z | 20 | 24 |

stimuli.title: Passage 3: A membrane as a concentration cell
stimuli.text:
A resting neuron membrane that is permeable mainly to K⁺ behaves like a concentration cell. At 37 °C the equilibrium potential for an ion of charge z is given by the Nernst equation:

E = (61.5 mV / z) log([ion]outside / [ion]inside)

In one experiment, students placed a cultured cell with 150 mM K⁺ inside in a bath with 5 mM K⁺ and measured the potential across its membrane with a microelectrode connected to a voltmeter. Before the run they checked the voltmeter against a zinc-copper galvanic cell, whose standard cell potential is +1.10 V for a reaction that transfers 2 electrons.

The lipid bilayer also stores charge like a parallel-plate capacitor. Its capacitance is about 1 µF for each square centimeter of membrane, and the charge it holds is Q = CV.

stimuli.title: Passage 4: Making and purifying aspirin
stimuli.text:
Students made aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, 180 g/mol) by heating salicylic acid (138 g/mol) with excess acetic anhydride and a few drops of sulfuric acid. Salicylic acid has a carboxylic acid group and a phenolic hydroxyl group on a benzene ring; the reaction converts one of them to an acetate ester and releases acetic acid.

Procedure:

1. React 2.76 g of salicylic acid, then add cold water to crystallize the crude product.
2. Dissolve the crude solid in diethyl ether and shake with aqueous sodium bicarbonate. Separate the layers, acidify the aqueous layer and collect the solid.
3. Recrystallize from a minimum volume of hot ethanol and water.
4. Test a few crystals with iron(III) chloride, which gives a violet color with phenols.
5. Check purity by thin-layer chromatography on silica gel.

The dry, recrystallized product weighed 2.70 g.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: Breathing gas at depth
stimuli.text:
Scuba divers breathe gas at the pressure of the water around them. Seawater has a density of about 1,025 kg/m³, and atmospheric pressure at the surface is 101 kPa. (Use g = 10 m/s².)

Three gas laws describe the main hazards. Boyle's law (P1V1 = P2V2 at constant temperature) explains why a diver who holds a breath while rising can overexpand the lungs. Dalton's law says each gas in a mixture contributes a partial pressure equal to its mole fraction times the total pressure; air is about 21% oxygen and 78% nitrogen. Henry's law says the amount of a gas that dissolves in a liquid is proportional to that gas's partial pressure above it.

For deep or long dives, some divers breathe heliox, a mixture of helium and oxygen, instead of air. Helium is chemically inert, has a low molar mass (4 g/mol compared with 28 g/mol for nitrogen) and is less soluble in body fat than nitrogen.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: Two inhibitors of one enzyme
stimuli.text:
Researchers measured the initial rate (v0) of an enzyme at several substrate concentrations, alone and in the presence of a fixed concentration of inhibitor X or inhibitor Y. The enzyme concentration was 0.010 µM in every assay, and the data fit the Michaelis-Menten equation, v0 = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]).

| [S] (mM) | v0, no inhibitor (µM/min) | v0 with X (µM/min) | v0 with Y (µM/min) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 33 | 14 | 17 |
| 2 | 50 | 25 | 25 |
| 6 | 75 | 50 | 38 |
| 18 | 90 | 75 | 45 |
| very high | 100 | 100 | 50 |

In separate experiments, dialysis removed inhibitor Y and fully restored activity.

stimuli.title: Passage 3: Imaging a fluorescent tag
stimuli.text:
Fluorescein, a dye used to label proteins, absorbs blue light most strongly at 490 nm and emits green light most strongly at 520 nm. After absorbing a photon, the excited molecule loses a little energy to its surroundings before it emits; the emitted photon therefore has less energy than the absorbed one. This difference is called the Stokes shift.

Labeled cells were viewed with a compound microscope: a 40x objective lens and a 10x eyepiece. To collect more light, the objective was used with immersion oil of refractive index 1.52 between the lens and the cover slip.

The energy of a photon is E = hc/λ; a convenient form is E (in eV) = 1,240 / λ (in nm). The speed of light in vacuum is 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

stimuli.title: Passage 4: From fat to soap
stimuli.text:
A triacylglycerol is an ester of glycerol, a three-carbon triol, with three fatty acids. Heating a fat with aqueous sodium hydroxide (saponification) breaks all three ester bonds. When the mixture is cooled and salt is added, the sodium salts of the fatty acids separate as soap.

In water, soap molecules gather into micelles above a certain concentration, and grease is carried away inside them. To identify the fatty acids in a sample, a chemist first converts them to methyl esters and then separates the esters by gas chromatography on a nonpolar column, where compounds elute roughly in order of boiling point.

| Fatty acid | Carbons | C=C bonds | Melting point (°C) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Palmitic | 16 | 0 | 63 |
| Stearic | 18 | 0 | 70 |
| Oleic (cis) | 18 | 1 | 13 |
| Linoleic (cis, cis) | 18 | 2 | -5 |

stimuli.title: Passage 1 (Humanities)
stimuli.text:
When a painting is cleaned, something is always lost. The question is only what. Old varnish yellows, dirt settles, and earlier restorers sometimes painted over damage with a heavy hand. A modern conservator can remove all of this and show us, we are told, the picture as the artist left it. The claim is attractive, and it is almost never true.

Consider what the artist actually left. Painters of the past knew that varnish would darken; some chose their colors with that in mind, and a few added thin tinted glazes over the paint itself. A solvent cannot always tell a later varnish from an original glaze. Strip the surface back to the brightest layer and you may expose colors that were never meant to be seen so raw. The cleaned picture is then not older than the dirty one; it is newer, a picture no one in the painter's lifetime ever saw.

There is a second loss, harder to name. A painting that has hung for four centuries has a history, and that history is written on its surface: the faint cracks, the softened edges, the warmth that time gives to whites. Those who favor thorough cleaning call these marks damage. I would call them evidence. We do not repaint the weathered stones of a cathedral to make it look as it did when the masons left, and few visitors would thank us if we did.

None of this means that nothing should be done. Grime that hides a figure, or a past repair that misrepresents the picture, may rightly be removed, and a varnish that is chemically failing threatens the paint beneath it. The conservator's first duty is to keep the object in being. But the goal should be legibility, not rejuvenation. A careful cleaning leaves a little of the old varnish in place, accepts some unevenness, and stops before certainty runs out.

The public enjoys a dramatic before-and-after photograph, and museums, which need visitors, enjoy providing one. That is precisely the danger. The most spectacular cleaning is not the most faithful, and an institution that measures success by how bright the result looks has already decided what the painting ought to be.

stimuli.title: Passage 2 (Social sciences)
stimuli.text:
For much of the twentieth century, economists told a simple story about shared resources. When many people draw on a pasture, a fishery or a forest that no one owns, each gains the full benefit of taking a little more while bearing only a fraction of the cost. The rational result, the story went, is ruin: the grass is grazed bare and the fish are gone. The cure was either private ownership or firm control by the state.

The story is not wrong so much as incomplete. Field researchers who looked closely at real fishing villages, irrigation systems and mountain pastures found many that had been used in common for centuries without collapse. What these places shared was not private title or a distant regulator but a set of local rules: who may fish, in which season, with what gear, and what happens to someone who cheats.

The rules that lasted had recognizable features. The users themselves helped write them, so the rules fit local conditions that an outsider would miss. Monitoring was cheap, often because the people doing it were users too, watching one another from neighboring boats. Penalties began small and grew only with repeated offenses, so that a single lapse did not turn a neighbor into an enemy. And there was some quick, local way to settle disputes.

These findings do not show that common ownership always works. Many commons have failed, especially where newcomers arrived faster than rules could adapt, or where a distant government overrode local arrangements without replacing them. The lesson is narrower and more useful: whether a shared resource survives depends less on who holds the title than on whether the people who use it can make, watch and enforce their own rules.

Policy has been slow to absorb this. A program that imposes a uniform national quota may look decisive, but if it displaces a working local system, it can leave a resource less protected than before.

stimuli.title: Passage 3 (Humanities)
stimuli.text:
It is often said that poetry is what gets lost in translation. The saying assumes that a poem is a fixed thing, a precise arrangement of sound and sense, and that any move into another language must spill some of it. On this view the translator is at best a careful porter, carrying the poem across a border and apologizing for the breakage.

The porter image fails because a poem's meaning is not a cargo that can be weighed before and after the trip. A line means what it does partly through rhythm, partly through the echoes its words carry in their own language, and partly through what readers bring to it. None of those can be packed. A translator must therefore choose, line by line, what to keep: the image, the music, the tone, the joke. Keeping all of them at once is usually impossible, and the choices differ for every poem.

This is why two good translations of the same poem can look so unlike each other, and why a weak original can sometimes become a stronger poem in a gifted translator's hands. The translator is not a porter but a second author, one who writes under unusual constraints. That is not a license for liberty; a translation that ignores its source has become something else, an imitation or a response. But it is a reason to judge translations as poems and not merely as copies.

Readers who know only one language are sometimes told that they cannot really read foreign poetry. I find this advice both snobbish and false. They cannot read the original, certainly, but they can read a poem that exists because of it, and their own language is enlarged by the encounter. Some of the most admired poems in any language began as translations.

stimuli.title: Passage 4 (Social sciences)
stimuli.text:
Before the railways, every town kept its own time. Noon was when the sun stood highest over the local church, and a traveler riding west found that his watch ran fast by a few minutes each day. No one minded much, because no one moved fast enough for the difference to matter.

The railways changed this, but not as quickly or as smoothly as the usual account suggests. Railway companies did adopt a single standard time for their timetables, because a train that left one station by local time and arrived at the next by another was an invitation to collisions. For decades afterward, however, many towns kept two times at once: railway time on the station clock and local time on the town hall. Courts in some places refused to recognize railway time in contracts, and newspapers printed tables for converting between the two.

What finally settled the matter was less the trains than the habits they created. Factories began to run to the whistle; schools rang bells on the hour; workers were paid for time rather than for tasks. A day once divided by light and weather came to be divided by the clock. Historians who describe this as a technical change, the spread of a better measurement, miss the larger point. Standard time was a social agreement, and like other agreements it was resisted, bargained over and, in the end, absorbed so completely that it came to seem natural.

This history matters because we still tend to treat clock time as simply the way time is. Shift workers whose bodies keep the sun's schedule, and communities that live by tides or seasons, are often described as poorly adapted. It would be more accurate to say that they live by an older agreement, and that the newer one won not because it was truer but because it served the interests of those who organized work.

stimuli.title: Passage 5 (Humanities)
stimuli.text:
Performers of early music like to say that they play what the composer wrote. The phrase sounds modest, but it hides a problem. For much of the music written before about 1750, what the composer wrote was not meant to be played as written. A melody line might be a sketch to be decorated; a bass line with a few figures beneath it asked the player to invent the harmony on the spot. The written page was less a script than a set of instructions for improvising.

Modern players who perform the page note for note are therefore not being faithful; they are performing a skeleton and calling it the body. The more historically minded performers know this and add ornaments, often taken from treatises of the period that explain how to decorate a line. But there is a trap here too. An ornament learned from a manual and played the same way every night is not improvisation; it is a new kind of score, written in the player's memory rather than on paper.

What the old practice asked for was not a particular set of notes but a particular relation between player and music: a willingness to take risks in front of listeners, to respond to the room, to play the same piece differently on Tuesday than on Monday. That relation is harder to recover than any ornament. It cannot be learned from a treatise, and it sits uneasily with a recording industry that prizes a flawless take.

I do not conclude that modern performances are false. A beautiful performance is a beautiful performance. But fidelity to the past is a stranger goal than its admirers suppose, and the most faithful player may be the one who is least concerned to repeat what anyone wrote down.

stimuli.title: Passage 1 (Social sciences)
stimuli.text:
Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists expect a large share to have no native speakers within a century. The usual response is documentation: record the last fluent speakers, write a grammar and a dictionary, and archive the results. Documentation is valuable, and in some cases it is the only thing that can be done. But it is often mistaken for a solution, and that mistake has consequences.

A language is not a list of words and rules; it is a practice, something people do with one another. An archive can preserve a description of the practice, much as a museum can preserve a costume. It cannot keep the practice alive, any more than the costume keeps the dance alive. When outside scholars treat documentation as the goal, they can leave communities with a well-catalogued record of what they have lost and little help in keeping it.

The revival efforts that have worked look different. They begin with the community rather than the archive, and they aim at use rather than record. Programs that pair elders with small children for whole days, so that the language is the medium of play and meals and not a school subject, have produced new young speakers in places where linguists had written the language off. Such programs are slow and costly, and they depend on adults willing to change the language of their own homes.

None of this makes documentation useless. A careful record can guide later learners, settle questions of pronunciation, and give a revival something to reach back to. The point is about order and purpose. Documentation serves revival when the community decides what to record and why; it replaces revival when the record becomes the end of the story.

stimuli.title: Passage 2 (Humanities)
stimuli.text:
Few buildings are as easy to dislike as the large concrete structures put up for governments and universities in the decades after the Second World War. Their surfaces stain, their plazas are windy, and their scale can make a visitor feel small. Many have already been demolished, and the loss is mourned by almost no one. I want to suggest that it should be.

The style was not born of indifference. Its designers were trying, often with very little money, to build public housing, libraries and civic halls quickly and in large numbers. They chose raw concrete partly because it was cheap and partly out of a kind of honesty: the building would show what it was made of and how it stood up, rather than dressing a frame in borrowed stone. Whatever one thinks of the results, the ambition behind them was generous.

Much of the hostility these buildings attract has less to do with their design than with their upkeep. Concrete that is cleaned and repaired weathers reasonably well; concrete that is neglected for forty years looks like a ruin. Many of these buildings were starved of maintenance by the same public bodies that commissioned them, and their decline is then offered as proof that they were bad from the start.

Taste in architecture changes on a cycle of about two generations. The ornate railway stations that one era tore down as vulgar, the next era fought to save. It would be a pity if we demolished the best concrete buildings of the last century just before our grandchildren learned to admire them. Keeping a building does not require liking it; it requires only the humility to suspect that our own judgment is not final.

stimuli.title: Passage 3 (Social sciences)
stimuli.text:
Economists have long found gift-giving puzzling. A gift transfers something the giver chose to someone whose tastes the giver can only guess. On average, surveys suggest, recipients would have paid less for their gifts than the gifts cost. Measured as a market exchange, the holiday season destroys value, and the rational thing would be to give cash.

Almost no one does, and the reason is not irrationality. A gift is not mainly a transfer of goods; it is a message about a relationship. Choosing an object takes time and attention, and the care shown in the choice is part of what is given. Cash, which can be handed over without any thought at all, sends the wrong message between friends, which is why it is acceptable from a grandparent to a child but awkward between equals.

Gifts also create obligations, and this is a feature rather than a flaw. Anthropologists who studied exchange in small societies found that a gift was expected to be returned, though not at once and not in kind. The delay kept the two parties connected: as long as a gift was owed, the relationship was open. A market purchase closes the account at the moment of payment; a gift keeps it open on purpose.

The market and the gift are not opposites so much as tools for different jobs. Businesses know this and borrow from the gift when they want loyalty rather than a single sale: the free sample, the unexpected upgrade, the handwritten note. Such gestures work only so long as they seem freely given. Once customers see them as a sales technique, they are judged by market standards again, and they usually fail those standards.

stimuli.title: Passage 4 (Humanities)
stimuli.text:
A narrator who cannot be trusted is one of fiction's oldest tools and one of its most misunderstood. The usual account treats the unreliable narrator as a puzzle: the narrator says one thing, the clues say another, and the attentive reader solves the case. On this account the pleasure of such books is the pleasure of being cleverer than the person speaking.

That pleasure is real, but it is the smaller part of what these books do. The best of them make the reader complicit before they make the reader wise. We spend a hundred pages inside the narrator's head, adopting his explanations, laughing at his jokes and sharing his irritation with the people around him. When the clues finally show us what he has been hiding, we discover not only that he was wrong but that we were content to be wrong with him.

The narrator in the novelist Harriet Vale's book about a retired schoolmaster is a good example. He tells us of his kindness to a former pupil, and we believe him, because his account is warm and detailed and flatters our wish to think well of teachers. Only late do we notice that every act of kindness he describes left the pupil more dependent on him. The discovery stings because we approved of each act as it was told.

Read this way, unreliable narration is less a game than a moral exercise. It shows how easily a fluent, sympathetic voice can carry us past what we would see at once from outside. Readers who treat such books only as puzzles to be solved protect themselves from that lesson, and so miss what the form is for.

stimuli.title: Passage 5 (Social sciences)
stimuli.text:
For most of their history, hospitals were places for the poor. A family with means was nursed at home, by its own servants and a visiting physician, and the hospital took in those who had no one: the sick traveler, the injured laborer, the widow without kin. Hospitals were run as charities, and patients were expected to show gratitude, obey the rules of the ward and, often, attend religious services.

The change came quickly once the hospital could offer what the home could not. Antiseptic surgery, then X-ray machines and laboratories, made the hospital the place where serious medicine was done. Paying patients began to arrive, and with them private rooms, admission fees and a new kind of institution. The charity ward did not disappear, but it sat beside the private wing, and the two were staffed and furnished differently.

Histories of this period usually describe it as a story of scientific progress, and in large part it was. But a second change happened at the same time and is easier to overlook. As the hospital became a place of technology, the patient became less a guest of the institution and more a case within it, defined by a diagnosis and a set of readings. The grateful pauper of the charity ward had at least been a person to whom something was owed. The modern patient, rich or poor, was increasingly a body on which procedures were done.

The movements of recent decades for patients' rights, informed consent and shared decision-making can be read as an attempt to undo this second change without giving up the first. They ask the hospital to remain a place of advanced medicine while treating the patient once again as someone with standing: a person whose understanding and agreement are part of the treatment rather than an obstacle to it.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: Taking apart a protease
stimuli.text:
Serine proteases cut peptide bonds using three active-site residues, a serine, a histidine and an aspartate. In the proposed mechanism, the histidine pulls a proton from the serine's hydroxyl group, and the activated serine oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon of the peptide bond, forming a short-lived tetrahedral intermediate. The aspartate holds the histidine in position. A separate pocket next to the active site binds the side chain of the residue just before the bond that is cut; in the enzyme studied, that pocket prefers large aromatic side chains such as phenylalanine.

Researchers replaced each active-site residue in turn and measured the kinetics of the purified enzymes at pH 8.0:

| Enzyme | kcat (s⁻¹) | Km (mM) |
|---|---|---|
| Wild type | 50 | 0.10 |
| Ser to Ala | 0.0005 | 0.12 |
| Asp to Asn | 0.5 | 0.11 |

The wild-type enzyme was most active between pH 7 and 9, and its activity fell steeply below pH 6.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: Switching on a stress gene
stimuli.text:
Cells exposed to a brief rise in temperature make large amounts of a protective protein called HRX. To learn how the HRX gene is controlled, researchers fused stretches of DNA from upstream of the gene to a reporter gene whose product glows, and measured light output after heat stress.

Experiment 1: Deleting a short sequence about 30 base pairs upstream of the transcription start site abolished reporter activity. Deleting a sequence 2,000 base pairs upstream cut heat-induced activity by 90%, and the same sequence still worked when it was flipped in orientation.

Experiment 2: A small interfering RNA (siRNA) matching the mRNA of a transcription factor, HSF, cut HSF protein by more than 80% and blocked the rise in HRX mRNA after heat.

Experiment 3: Cells treated with cycloheximide, which blocks translation, still raised HRX mRNA after heat stress.

The HRX gene spans about 6 kilobases of DNA, while the mature HRX mRNA is about 1.8 kilobases long.

stimuli.title: Passage 3: When DNA is damaged
stimuli.text:
Ultraviolet light damages DNA, mostly by linking adjacent pyrimidines on the same strand. In healthy cells the damage triggers a rise in the protein p53, which acts as a transcription factor. One of its targets encodes p21, a protein that inhibits the cyclin-dependent kinases that drive cells from G1 into S phase. If the damage is too great to repair, p53 also turns on genes that start apoptosis, a controlled form of cell death in which mitochondria release cytochrome c into the cytoplasm.

Researchers exposed two cultured cell lines to the same dose of UV light. Line A has two working copies of the gene for p53; line B has none. Twelve hours later, 70% of line A cells were held in G1 and 10% were undergoing apoptosis. In line B, fewer than 5% were held in G1, almost none were undergoing apoptosis, and the cells kept dividing. Over the following weeks, line B accumulated many more mutations than line A.

stimuli.title: Passage 4: Two patients who cannot concentrate their urine
stimuli.text:
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) helps the body hold on to water. It is made by neurons of the hypothalamus and released into the blood when plasma osmolality rises. In the kidney it acts on the collecting ducts, which pass through a medulla whose interstitial fluid is made very salty by the loops of Henle.

Two patients who passed large volumes of dilute urine underwent a water deprivation test, followed by an injection of desmopressin, a synthetic drug that acts like ADH. Urine osmolality was measured at the end of each stage:

| Person | After water deprivation (mOsm/kg) | After desmopressin (mOsm/kg) |
|---|---|---|
| Healthy volunteer | 900 | 950 |
| Patient 1 | 150 | 700 |
| Patient 2 | 150 | 160 |

During deprivation, both patients' plasma sodium rose above the normal range and both reported intense thirst.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: A child who cannot fast
stimuli.text:
A two-year-old boy became shaky and drowsy whenever he went more than three or four hours without food. Tests showed a low blood glucose, a high blood lactate and a greatly enlarged liver packed with glycogen. Genetic testing found that he lacks working glucose-6-phosphatase, an enzyme in the endoplasmic reticulum of liver cells that removes the phosphate from glucose 6-phosphate so that free glucose can leave the cell.

During a supervised fast, physicians injected glucagon, which normally raises blood glucose within minutes by signaling liver cells to break down glycogen. The boy's blood glucose did not rise, but his blood lactate rose further.

He was started on frequent meals by day and uncooked cornstarch, a slowly digested starch, at night. With this diet his fasting glucose stayed in the normal range.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: Testing a family for a muscle disease
stimuli.text:
A muscle-wasting disease in one family is caused by a deletion in a gene on the X chromosome. The disease is recessive. The family's first son is affected; his father is unaffected and his mother shows no symptoms.

To test other family members, a laboratory used the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with primers on either side of the deletion. The normal allele gives a 450 base-pair product and the deleted allele a 300 base-pair product. The products were separated by agarose gel electrophoresis, with DNA loaded in wells at the negative electrode.

| Family member | Bands seen (bp) |
|---|---|
| Mother | 450 and 300 |
| Affected son | 300 |
| Daughter | 450 and 300 |
| Second son | 450 |

stimuli.title: Passage 3: Blocking a retrovirus
stimuli.text:
HIV is an enveloped retrovirus whose genome is two copies of single-stranded RNA. After the virus binds CD4 and a co-receptor on a helper T cell, its core enters the cell, and the viral enzyme reverse transcriptase copies the RNA genome into double-stranded DNA. A second viral enzyme, integrase, inserts that DNA into a host chromosome, where it is transcribed by the host's RNA polymerase. Viral proteins are first made as long polyproteins that the viral protease cuts into working pieces as new particles bud from the cell.

Zidovudine (AZT), one of the first anti-HIV drugs, is an analog of the nucleoside thymidine in which the 3' hydroxyl group of the sugar is replaced by an azido group. Protease inhibitors were added later. Treatment with a single drug usually failed within months because resistant virus appeared; combinations of drugs from different classes suppressed the virus for years.

stimuli.title: Passage 4: Weakness that grows with effort
stimuli.text:
At the neuromuscular junction, an action potential reaching the motor neuron's terminal opens voltage-gated calcium channels. Calcium entry causes vesicles of acetylcholine (ACh) to fuse with the membrane. ACh crosses the cleft, binds nicotinic receptors on the muscle fiber and opens their ion channels, depolarizing the fiber. Acetylcholinesterase in the cleft breaks ACh down within milliseconds.

In myasthenia gravis, antibodies against the nicotinic receptor reduce the number of working receptors. Patients have muscle weakness that worsens with repeated use, such as drooping eyelids late in the day. Normally, the depolarization produced at the junction is well above the threshold needed to fire a muscle action potential, and the amount of ACh released falls slightly with each impulse in a rapid series.

A patient's grip strength was measured before and two minutes after an injection of a short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; it rose from 12 kg to 25 kg.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: Sleep after learning
stimuli.text:
A team of researchers tested whether sleep after learning helps memory. Sixty college students learned a list of 40 word pairs at 9 p.m. and were then randomly assigned to one of two groups. The sleep group slept normally in the laboratory; the wake group stayed awake under supervision until the next evening. Both groups then had a full night of recovery sleep, and recall was tested 36 hours after learning, so that neither group was tired at the test.

The sleep group recalled 70% of the pairs and the wake group 45%. Recordings in the sleep group showed that recall was best in students who spent the most time in slow-wave sleep during the first night. During the night awake, the wake group also missed more targets on a task that asked them to press a key whenever a rare letter appeared in a stream of common ones, and they rated themselves as more irritable. Several drank coffee to stay awake; the researchers recorded caffeine intake but did not control it.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: Going along with the group
stimuli.text:
In a series of studies, a participant sat with several other people who appeared to be fellow participants but were in fact working for the researcher. On each trial the group was shown a reference line and three comparison lines and asked which comparison matched the reference. The answer was obvious, but on most trials the others all gave the same wrong answer before the participant responded.

When participants answered aloud, they gave the group's wrong answer on 32% of trials. When they wrote their answers privately after hearing the group, the rate fell to 8%. Conformity rose as the group grew from one to three others but changed little beyond that. When one of the others gave the correct answer before the participant, conformity dropped to about 6%. In interviews afterward, many participants who had conformed said they did not want to seem odd or to spoil the session for the others.

In a follow-up, observers watched videos of conforming participants and were asked to explain their behavior. Most said the participants were simply weak-willed or easily led.

stimuli.title: Passage 3: Two neighborhoods, one city
stimuli.text:
In a mid-sized city, average life expectancy in the Riverside district is 12 years lower than in the Hilltop district, three miles away. Riverside was among the areas that banks once refused to lend in, and for decades its residents were mostly people who could not buy homes elsewhere. Today it has more households below the poverty line, fewer grocery stores selling fresh food, and an interstate highway and a waste transfer station along its edge. Hilltop has none of these.

Riverside also has more children per family and fewer residents over 65. In the past decade, rising rents in the city center have brought young professionals into the part of Riverside nearest downtown, and some long-time residents there have moved out because they can no longer afford to stay.

A local health department report argued that the gap in life expectancy could not be explained by individual choices about diet and exercise alone, and that the history and layout of the city shaped the health of the people who lived in it.

stimuli.title: Passage 4: Paying people to quit smoking
stimuli.text:
Researchers tested a smartphone program to help adults quit smoking. Each day, participants blew into a small device that measures carbon monoxide in the breath, which confirms recent smoking. For 12 weeks, participants in Group 1 earned 10 points, worth a small cash value, on every smoke-free day. Participants in Group 2 had the chance to earn points on a smoke-free day, but whether they won, and how much, depended on an unpredictable draw. Both groups were also sent short daily messages about the health effects of smoking, some written in general terms and some tailored to the participant's own health history.

During the 12 weeks, both groups had far more smoke-free days than a control group. After the rewards stopped, many participants in both groups returned to smoking, but relapse was slower in Group 2. Participants who kept smoking during the program were more likely than others to agree with statements such as "The health risks of smoking are exaggerated." Participants who said they cared most about their health read the tailored messages more carefully and changed their attitudes toward smoking more than other participants.

stimuli.title: Passage 1: What we fail to see
stimuli.text:
In an experiment on visual attention, participants watched a one-minute video of two teams passing basketballs. Half were told to count the passes made by one team (counting group); the other half were told only to watch the video (watching group). Halfway through, a person carrying an open red umbrella walked slowly across the scene for five seconds. Afterward, participants were asked whether they had noticed anything unusual.

In the watching group, 95% reported the umbrella; in the counting group, only 45% did. In a third condition, participants counted passes but were told beforehand that something unexpected might appear, and 80% reported the umbrella.

In a separate task, participants saw a smudged figure that could be read as either the letter B or the number 13. When it was shown between the letters A and C, most read it as B; between 12 and 14, most read it as 13.

In a final condition, participants in the counting group watched in small groups that included one confederate, who said loudly at the end, "Nothing unusual happened." Fewer participants in these groups reported the umbrella than counting participants who watched alone.

stimuli.title: Passage 2: The same résumé, different names
stimuli.text:
To study hiring discrimination, researchers sent pairs of fictional résumés to employers advertising entry-level jobs. The résumés in each pair had the same education and experience; only the name differed, chosen to suggest an applicant from either a majority or a minority ethnic group. Résumés with majority-group names received 50% more requests for interviews.

The researchers then surveyed a sample of the hiring managers. Most said they valued diversity and rejected stereotypes. But on a timed computer task that measures how quickly people pair group images with positive or negative words, many responded faster when minority-group images were paired with negative words.

In one company, a hiring committee of long-time colleagues reported that it always reached decisions quickly and without disagreement, even when members later admitted privately that they had had doubts. The company then asked managers to sign a short pledge to review résumés with names hidden; a month later, managers who had signed were more likely than others to volunteer for a longer anti-bias training. A separate program paired managers from different backgrounds to work as equal partners on a shared project for six months.

stimuli.title: Passage 3: A changing population
stimuli.text:
The table shows crude birth and death rates (per 1,000 people per year) in a hypothetical country over six decades. Net migration was close to zero throughout.

| Year | Crude birth rate | Crude death rate |
|---|---|---|
| 1950 | 42 | 25 |
| 1970 | 38 | 12 |
| 1990 | 24 | 9 |
| 2010 | 12 | 10 |

Over the same period the country industrialized. The share of people living in cities rose from 20% to 70%, the share of girls finishing secondary school rose from 10% to 85%, and the share of workers employed in farming fell from 70% to 15%. Many children of farm families became factory workers, clerks or teachers. A government survey found that by 2010 most people in professional jobs had parents who had worked on farms.

stimuli.title: Passage 4: Treating depression
stimuli.text:
Researchers randomly assigned 300 adults with major depressive disorder to 16 weeks of one of three treatments: a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), or a pill with no active ingredient (placebo). Neither the participants nor the doctors who rated their symptoms knew who was taking the drug and who the placebo. Symptoms improved substantially in 55% of the SSRI group, 52% of the CBT group and 30% of the placebo group.

The same team also studied twins. When one identical twin had major depressive disorder, the other also had it in about 40% of pairs; for fraternal twins the figure was about 20%.

Participants with higher scores on a personality measure of anxiety, moodiness and emotional instability at the start of the study were more likely to relapse in the year after treatment. Many participants also described having stopped trying to change things in their lives after repeated failures they felt they could not control.

questions.stem: What is the mean flow speed in the narrowed segment?
questions.explanation: Continuity gives A1v1 = A2v2, and area goes with r squared, so halving the radius makes the area a quarter and the speed four times larger: 4 x 0.30 = 1.2 m/s. Doubling the speed (0.60 m/s) treats speed as if it scaled with radius.

questions.stem: Ignoring viscosity, by about how much is the pressure in the narrowed segment lower than the upstream pressure?
questions.explanation: Bernoulli's equation for a horizontal tube gives ΔP = ½ρ(v2² - v1²) = 0.5 x 1,060 x (1.44 - 0.09) ≈ 720 Pa. Leaving out the factor of one half gives about 1,430 Pa.

questions.stem: In a long vessel obeying Poiseuille's law, the radius is halved while the pressure difference stays the same. The volume flow rate:
questions.explanation: Flow depends on r to the fourth power, so halving r divides Q by 2⁴ = 16. A factor of 1/4 would follow if flow depended on cross-sectional area alone.

questions.stem: A condition raises blood viscosity by 50% with no change in vessel size. To keep the same flow through a long vessel, the pressure difference must become:
questions.explanation: In Poiseuille's law Q is proportional to ΔP/η, so if η rises by a factor of 1.5, ΔP must rise by the same factor to hold Q constant. Squaring the factor (2.25) would apply only to a quantity that varies with η squared.

questions.stem: In a standing person, an artery in the foot lies 1.2 m below the heart. How much greater is the blood pressure there because of the column of blood alone? (Use g = 10 m/s².)
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic pressure is ρgh = 1,060 x 10 x 1.2 ≈ 12,700 Pa, or 12.7 kPa. A value of 1.3 kPa leaves out the factor of g.

questions.stem: What is the arterial pH of Patient X?
questions.explanation: Dissolved CO2 is 0.03 x 80 = 2.4 mM, so pH = 6.1 + log(24/2.4) = 6.1 + 1 = 7.1. A pH of 7.4 is Patient W, whose PaCO2 is half as high.

questions.stem: Patient Z's values point to which acid-base disturbance?
questions.explanation: Z's PaCO2 is half of normal with normal bicarbonate, so the ratio and the pH rise (pH 7.7), and the cause is breathing off too much CO2. A metabolic alkalosis would start with a high bicarbonate.

questions.stem: What does carbonic anhydrase do to the reaction between CO2 and water?
options: Raises the pKa of the acid
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse reactions alike, so equilibrium is reached faster but its position is unchanged. It does not alter ΔG or the acid's pKa.

questions.stem: The buffer's apparent pKa of 6.1 is far from normal blood pH, yet the system buffers blood well. The best explanation is that:
options: the lungs can remove the CO2 formed
its pKa equals normal blood pH
bicarbonate acts as a very strong base
questions.explanation: The bicarbonate system is open: acid added to blood converts bicarbonate to CO2, which is breathed out, so the acid does not build up. A closed buffer works best within about one pH unit of its pKa.

questions.stem: Which change would bring Patient Y's pH closest to normal within minutes?
questions.explanation: Y has a metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate halved). Breathing faster lowers PaCO2, which raises the bicarbonate-to-CO2 ratio and the pH within minutes; the kidneys act over hours to days, and both renal changes listed would lower pH further.

questions.stem: During hard exercise, lactic acid releases H⁺ into the blood. What is the immediate effect on the equilibrium in the passage?
options: The pKa of the system falls
questions.explanation: Added H⁺ combines with HCO3⁻, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts toward H2CO3 and CO2. The pKa is a constant and does not change.

questions.stem: What membrane potential does the Nernst equation predict for the cell in the experiment?
questions.explanation: E = 61.5 log(5/150) = 61.5 x (-1.48) ≈ -91 mV: the inside is negative because K⁺ leaks out down its gradient. A positive value comes from flipping the ratio.

questions.stem: If the K⁺ concentration in the bath rose to 10 mM, the predicted potential would be about:
questions.explanation: E = 61.5 log(10/150) = 61.5 x (-1.18) ≈ -72 mV. Raising outside K⁺ narrows the gradient, so the potential becomes less negative, which is why high blood potassium depolarizes cells.

questions.stem: How much charge is stored on 1.0 cm² of membrane held at 90 mV?
questions.explanation: Q = CV = (1 x 10⁻⁶ F)(0.090 V) = 9 x 10⁻⁸ C. Using 90 V instead of 0.090 V gives the answer 1,000 times too large.

questions.stem: For an accurate reading, the voltmeter connected to the microelectrode should have:
options: a resistance equal to the cell's
questions.explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel and should draw almost no current, so it needs a very high resistance; a low resistance would drain the very potential it measures.

questions.stem: What is the standard free energy change of the zinc-copper reaction used to check the voltmeter?
questions.explanation: ΔG° = -nFE° = -2 x 96,485 x 1.10 ≈ -212,000 J/mol = -212 kJ/mol; a positive cell potential means a spontaneous reaction and a negative ΔG°. Using n = 1 gives -106 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: Which group of salicylic acid reacts with acetic anhydride to make aspirin?
questions.explanation: Aspirin is the acetate ester of the phenol: the -OH on the ring is acetylated, and the carboxylic acid is left free. That is why the product still dissolves in bicarbonate.

questions.stem: In step 2, where is the aspirin just before the layers are separated?
options: In the aqueous layer, as the acid
In the ether layer, as its salt
In the aqueous layer, as its salt
In the ether layer, as the acid
questions.explanation: Bicarbonate deprotonates the carboxylic acid, and the charged carboxylate dissolves in water rather than ether. Acidifying the aqueous layer afterward turns it back into the neutral acid, which precipitates.

questions.stem: On the silica gel plate in step 5, the compound that travels farthest is the one that:
options: dissolves least in the moving eluent
questions.explanation: Silica is a polar stationary phase, so a compound that binds it weakly spends more time in the moving solvent and has a higher Rf. More polar compounds stick to the silica and move less.

questions.stem: After recrystallization, a few crystals still turn violet with iron(III) chloride. This shows that:
questions.explanation: Iron(III) chloride reacts with a free phenolic -OH, which aspirin lacks once acetylated. A violet color means unreacted salicylic acid is still present.

questions.stem: What is the percent yield of the recrystallized aspirin?
questions.explanation: 2.76 g / 138 g/mol = 0.0200 mol of salicylic acid, so the theoretical yield is 0.0200 x 180 = 3.60 g, and 2.70 / 3.60 = 75%. Dividing 2.70 g by the 2.76 g of starting material ignores the change in molar mass.

questions.stem: Old aspirin tablets stored in humid air often smell of vinegar. The most likely reason is that:
options: the ester hydrolyzes to acetic acid
the phenol group is acetylated again
questions.explanation: Water slowly hydrolyzes the ester back to salicylic acid and acetic acid, and acetic acid gives vinegar its smell. Benzene rings are not reduced under such mild conditions.

questions.stem: A 2.0 kg cast is lifted straight up 0.50 m at constant speed in 2.0 s. What average power is delivered? (Use g = 10 m/s².)
questions.explanation: Work against gravity is mgh = 2.0 x 10 x 0.50 = 10 J, and power is work divided by time: 10 J / 2.0 s = 5 W. The 10 W answer gives the work, not the rate.

questions.stem: An object is 30 cm from a converging lens with a focal length of 10 cm. How far from the lens is the image?
questions.explanation: From 1/f = 1/do + 1/di, 1/di = 1/10 - 1/30 = 2/30, so di = 15 cm on the far side (a real, inverted image). Adding the reciprocals instead gives 7.5 cm.

questions.stem: A tracer with a half-life of 6.0 hours is injected. What percent of its activity remains after 24 hours?
questions.explanation: Twenty-four hours is four half-lives, so the fraction left is (1/2)⁴ = 1/16 = 6.25%. Three half-lives would leave 12.5%.

questions.stem: Which of these compounds of similar molar mass has the highest boiling point?
questions.explanation: Ethanol has an O-H group and forms hydrogen bonds between molecules, which take the most energy to overcome. Dimethyl ether is polar but has no O-H, and propane has only dispersion forces.

questions.stem: A reaction has ΔH = -40 kJ/mol and ΔS = -100 J/(mol·K). Under standard conditions it is spontaneous:
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS is negative while TΔS is less negative than ΔH, that is while T < 40,000/100 = 400 K. Above that, the unfavorable entropy term wins.

questions.stem: Glycine has pKa values of 2.34 (carboxyl group) and 9.60 (amino group). What is its isoelectric point?
questions.explanation: For an amino acid with no ionizable side chain, the pI is the average of the two pKa values: (2.34 + 9.60) / 2 = 5.97. At that pH the zwitterion carries no net charge.

questions.stem: Calcium fluoride (CaF2) has Ksp = 3.9 × 10⁻¹¹. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
questions.explanation: CaF2 dissolves to s of Ca²⁺ and 2s of F⁻, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³ and s = (9.75 x 10⁻¹²)^(1/3) ≈ 2.1 x 10⁻⁴ M. Taking the square root of Ksp treats it as a 1:1 salt.

questions.stem: A molecule has three chirality centers and no internal plane of symmetry. How many stereoisomers can it have?
questions.explanation: With n chirality centers and no meso forms, the maximum number of stereoisomers is 2ⁿ = 2³ = 8. Multiplying 3 by 2 gives 6, which undercounts.

questions.stem: The central claim of the passage is that the cleaning of old paintings should aim to:
options: return the picture to the very day it was finished
remove every later varnish and repair
make the picture legible while keeping its history
questions.explanation: The author says the goal should be legibility, not rejuvenation, and treats the marks of age as evidence worth keeping. Restoring the picture as it was on the day it was finished is the claim the author calls almost never true.

questions.stem: In the passage, the author's statement that the fully cleaned picture is "newer" than the dirty one means that it:
options: shows a surface no one saw in the painter's day
was painted later than experts believed
has been varnished again after cleaning
will darken again much more quickly than before
questions.explanation: The author argues that stripping to the brightest layer can remove original glazes, producing "a picture no one in the painter's lifetime ever saw." Nothing in the passage concerns repainting or dating the work.

questions.stem: The comparison with the weathered stones of a cathedral serves mainly to:
options: suggest that old cathedrals need cleaning too
prove that varnish protects paint layers
show that visitors prefer new buildings
show that marks of age are usually accepted
questions.explanation: The author uses the cathedral to argue by analogy that we normally accept the traces of age on old objects and would not thank anyone for erasing them. It is not offered as evidence about varnish chemistry.

questions.stem: Which statement about cleaning would the author be most likely to accept?
options: Any cleaning harms the original paint
Dirt that hides a figure should stay
Removing a failing varnish can be justified
Every past repair should always be kept in place
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph allows that a chemically failing varnish threatens the paint and may rightly be removed, along with misleading repairs and grime that hides a figure. The author is not against all cleaning.

questions.stem: Suppose a museum leaves a thin, even layer of old varnish on a cleaned portrait and labels the result as deliberately restrained. Based on the passage, the author would most likely regard this as:
options: an attempt to stage a dramatic before-and-after
a sound choice that stops before certainty runs out
a failure to show the portrait's true colors
a sign that the museum lacks the right kind of solvent
questions.explanation: Leaving some old varnish and accepting unevenness is exactly what the author describes as careful cleaning. The author criticizes the opposite, the bright spectacular result.

questions.stem: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's argument about original glazes?
options: Solvents can reliably tell varnish from glaze
Many old varnishes yellow within fifty years
Most visitors prefer brightly cleaned paintings
questions.explanation: Part of the argument rests on the claim that a solvent cannot always tell a later varnish from an original glaze. If conservators could reliably separate them, that risk would largely disappear. Visitor preferences are what the author already concedes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the commons that lasted for centuries had in common:
options: strict control by a distant national government
a single owner holding private title
local rules that users made and enforced
questions.explanation: The second and third paragraphs say these places shared not private title or a distant regulator but local rules on access, seasons and gear, written and enforced by the users.

questions.stem: The author describes the older economic story about shared resources as:
options: a myth with no basis at all
correct in every single case it covered
questions.explanation: The second paragraph opens, "The story is not wrong so much as incomplete": overuse can happen, but the story leaves out the local rules that often prevent it.

questions.stem: The author mentions commons that failed after newcomers arrived mainly in order to:
options: limit the scope of the conclusion
show that private title always works
prove the older story was right
questions.explanation: The failures are a qualification: the author concedes that common use does not always succeed and narrows the lesson to whether users can make, watch and enforce their own rules.

questions.stem: A village irrigation system has run for generations under rules set by its farmers. A new law replaces those rules with a uniform national schedule. Based on the passage, the most likely result is that the water supply will be:
options: privately owned by the farmers alone
questions.explanation: The final paragraph warns that a uniform national program that displaces a working local system can leave a resource less protected than before. Nothing suggests the law would create private title.

questions.stem: Which of the following rules for a shared forest best fits the features the author says successful rules have?
options: Rules written by a distant agency
A large fine for any first offense
Monitoring that is paid for and run by outsiders
Small fines that rise with repeat offenses
questions.explanation: The third paragraph lists graduated penalties that begin small and grow only with repeated offenses, rules users help write, and cheap monitoring by users themselves. A large fine for a first lapse is the opposite of graduated penalties.

questions.stem: The author's main purpose in the passage is to argue that a translator of poetry is best understood as:
options: an imitator who ignores the original source
a porter carrying a fixed cargo
a second author working under constraints
questions.explanation: The third paragraph states that the translator "is not a porter but a second author, one who writes under unusual constraints." The porter is the view the author rejects.

questions.stem: The author's point that two good translations of one poem can look very unlike each other is offered as evidence that:
options: the original poem was badly written
one of the two must be a poor translation
translators must choose what to keep
questions.explanation: Because no translation can keep image, music, tone and joke at once, each translator chooses differently, which is why good translations diverge. The author does not say one must be poor.

questions.stem: The author's view of the advice that readers of one language "cannot really read foreign poetry" is best described as:
options: uncertain, noting a lack of solid evidence
dismissive, calling it snobbish and false
questions.explanation: The author writes, "I find this advice both snobbish and false," and argues that such readers read a real poem that exists because of the original.

questions.stem: A writer publishes a poem that keeps only the title and one image of a famous original and otherwise says something new. Based on the passage, the author would most likely call it:
options: an imitation or a response, not a translation
a model of the second author at work
a faithful copy of the original poem
proof that poetry is always lost in translation
questions.explanation: The author warns that the second-author view is not a license for liberty: "a translation that ignores its source has become something else, an imitation or a response."

questions.stem: The author's reasoning about translation would apply most directly to which other situation?
options: Converting a measurement from feet to meters
Staging a play written for a very different theater
Copying a document for a legal archive
Reprinting an old novel with its typing errors corrected
questions.explanation: Like a poem, a play's meaning depends on elements that cannot all be carried over, so a director must choose what to keep and acts as a kind of second author. A unit conversion or a faithful copy has an exact result and needs no such choices.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did railway companies adopt a single standard time?
options: Factories asked them to do so
Courts required it in every contract
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says a train leaving one station by local time and arriving at the next by another "was an invitation to collisions." Courts in some places in fact refused to recognize railway time.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, for decades after railways adopted standard time, many towns:
options: kept railway and local time side by side
set every clock by the sun at noon
banned railway time from their stations
questions.explanation: The author describes towns with railway time on the station clock and local time on the town hall, with newspapers printing conversion tables. The change was neither quick nor smooth.

questions.stem: The author criticizes historians who describe standard time as a technical change because they:
options: exaggerate the role played by the railways
ignore the accuracy of solar time
overlook that it was a social agreement
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says such historians "miss the larger point. Standard time was a social agreement," resisted, bargained over and finally absorbed.

questions.stem: Which assumption underlies the author's final claim about shift workers?
options: Shift work is unhealthy for most people
Clock time is more accurate than solar time
How a society keeps time reflects choices
Tidal communities refuse to use clocks
questions.explanation: The author says such workers live by an older agreement that lost not because it was less true but because the newer one served those who organized work. That only follows if a time system is a choice rather than a fact of nature.

questions.stem: A company introduces software that tracks employees' work minute by minute and pays by logged time. The author would most likely see this as:
options: a continuation of the clock's rise in work
a purely technical improvement in measurement
evidence that standard time was never needed
a return to tasks set by light and weather
questions.explanation: The passage ties standard time to factories running to the whistle and workers paid for time rather than tasks. Minute-by-minute tracking extends that same arrangement, and the author rejects calling such changes purely technical.

questions.stem: Which discovery would most challenge the author's account of how standard time took hold?
options: Some local courts were slow to accept railway time
Towns adopted it before factory schedules spread
questions.explanation: The author argues that the habits of work, not the trains themselves, settled the matter. If towns had fully adopted standard time before factory schedules spread, that causal claim would be weakened. Slow courts and resistant workers fit the account.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, a melody line that is "a sketch to be decorated" is one that the composer expected performers to:
options: add notes of their own to
questions.explanation: The author explains that such a line was "a sketch to be decorated" and the page "a set of instructions for improvising," so performers were expected to add ornaments.

questions.stem: Why does the author regard an ornament learned from a treatise and played the same way every night as a trap?
options: It removes the bass line's harmony
It makes the music too difficult
It turns improvising into a new score
questions.explanation: The author says such an ornament "is not improvisation; it is a new kind of score, written in the player's memory." The objection is to fixed repetition, not to the treatise's accuracy.

questions.stem: A harpsichordist plays a seventeenth-century piece with different decorations at each concert, depending on how the audience responds. The author would most likely regard this as:
options: a skeleton presented as the body
close to what the old practice asked for
unfaithful because it changes the written score
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the old practice asked for a willingness to respond to the room and to play the piece differently on different days. Playing the bare written notes is what the author calls a skeleton.

questions.stem: Which new information would most strengthen the author's claim about the recording industry?
options: Many performers also teach at music conservatories
Early music recordings sell less than jazz
Labels routinely splice takes to remove risks
questions.explanation: The author says the old practice sits uneasily with an industry that prizes a flawless take. Evidence that labels routinely edit out risky moments would directly support that claim; sales or audio quality bear on it only loosely.

questions.stem: The author's argument about fidelity in early music is most similar to which claim?
options: Old instruments sound better than new ones
Following a recipe exactly can miss a cook's way
A photograph is always more accurate than a painting
A score should be played at the written tempo
questions.explanation: The author argues that literal fidelity to a written text can miss what the practice behind it asked for. A recipe followed to the letter that loses the cook's own improvising makes the same point.

questions.stem: In the proposed mechanism, what role does the active-site serine play?
options: It binds the substrate's side chain
It attacks the peptide carbonyl carbon
It holds the histidine in place
It donates a proton to the leaving group
questions.explanation: The passage says the activated serine oxygen attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming the tetrahedral intermediate, so serine is the nucleophile. Holding the histidine in place is the aspartate's job.

questions.stem: The data for the serine-to-alanine enzyme suggest that the serine is needed mainly for:
questions.explanation: kcat falls 100,000-fold (50 to 0.0005 per second) while Km barely changes (0.10 to 0.12 mM), so the substrate still binds but is not turned over. A binding defect would show up as a large rise in Km.

questions.stem: By about what factor is the catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km) of the wild-type enzyme greater than that of the aspartate-to-asparagine enzyme?
questions.explanation: Wild type: 50 / 0.10 = 500 per mM per second. Asp to Asn: 0.5 / 0.11 ≈ 4.5. The ratio is 500 / 4.5 ≈ 110. Comparing kcat alone would give 100.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the drop in activity below pH 6?
options: The aspartate gains a negative charge
Peptide bonds hydrolyze on their own
questions.explanation: Histidine's side chain has a pKa near 6, so below pH 6 it is mostly protonated and can no longer accept the serine's proton. Serine's hydroxyl is far too weak an acid to lose a proton at low pH.

questions.stem: Why is alanine a good choice to replace the active-site serine in this kind of study?
options: It adds a positive charge to the site
It removes the hydroxyl but keeps the size
It is the largest nonpolar amino acid
It forms a disulfide bond with the histidine
questions.explanation: Alanine's side chain is a methyl group, so the swap removes only serine's -OH and keeps the shape nearly the same, isolating the role of the hydroxyl. Alanine is small and uncharged.

questions.stem: Based on its substrate preference, the side-chain binding pocket of this enzyme is most likely lined with:
questions.explanation: Large aromatic side chains such as phenylalanine are nonpolar, so they fit best in a hydrophobic pocket. A negatively charged pocket would favor basic residues like lysine instead.

questions.stem: The sequence about 30 base pairs upstream of the start site, whose loss abolished all activity, is most likely part of the:
questions.explanation: Elements near -30, such as the TATA box, help position RNA polymerase II at the start site, so without them transcription fails. The distant sequence that still worked when flipped behaves like an enhancer.

questions.stem: The sequence 2,000 base pairs upstream is best classified as an enhancer because it:
options: is translated into a short peptide
is required for any transcription at all
works far away and in either orientation
questions.explanation: Enhancers raise transcription from a distance and independent of orientation, as the flipped sequence did. Loss of all transcription was the effect of the core promoter deletion, not this one.

questions.stem: How did the siRNA in Experiment 2 most likely reduce HSF protein?
options: It blocked transcription of every gene
It led to degradation of HSF mRNA
It bound HSF protein and blocked it
It deleted the HSF gene from DNA
questions.explanation: An siRNA guides a protein complex to the matching mRNA, which is cut or silenced, so less protein is made. It does not change the DNA or bind the protein itself.

questions.stem: What does Experiment 3 suggest about how heat stress turns on the HRX gene?
options: New HSF protein must be made first
HRX mRNA is made without transcription
The activating factor already exists in the cell
Translation of HRX protein is not needed for survival
questions.explanation: HRX mRNA still rose when new protein synthesis was blocked, so the factor that switches the gene on must already be present and is activated by heat rather than newly made.

questions.stem: Why is the mature HRX mRNA much shorter than the stretch of DNA the gene spans?
options: The poly(A) tail is cut off
Only one DNA strand is copied
questions.explanation: The primary transcript contains introns that the spliceosome removes, joining the exons into a shorter mature mRNA. Copying only one strand does not shorten the product.

questions.stem: At which point in the cell cycle were most line A cells held after UV exposure?
questions.explanation: p21 inhibits the kinases that drive cells from G1 into S, so damaged cells stop before replicating their DNA, as 70% of line A did.

questions.stem: Based on its role in the passage, the gene for p53 is best classed as:
questions.explanation: p53 halts division and triggers apoptosis after damage, so losing its function, as in line B, lets damaged cells keep dividing: the mark of a tumor suppressor. A proto-oncogene promotes division and causes cancer when it becomes overactive.

questions.stem: In the apoptosis described in the passage, cytochrome c is released from:
options: the lumen of the rough endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c normally carries electrons between complexes on the inner membrane and sits in the intermembrane space; its release into the cytoplasm starts the caspase cascade.

questions.stem: Why did line B accumulate more mutations than line A over the following weeks?
options: It divided without pausing to repair
It repaired damage more slowly in S phase
It lost all its DNA polymerases
questions.explanation: Without p53, line B neither arrested in G1 nor underwent apoptosis, so damaged cells copied unrepaired DNA and passed the errors on. Both lines received the same UV dose.

questions.stem: Which repair pathway mainly removes the pyrimidine dimers caused by UV light?
questions.explanation: Bulky lesions that distort the helix, such as pyrimidine dimers, are cut out with a short stretch of the strand and the gap filled in. Mismatch repair corrects replication errors between normal bases.

questions.stem: Where is ADH released into the bloodstream?
questions.explanation: Hypothalamic neurons make ADH and carry it down their axons to the posterior pituitary, which releases it. The anterior pituitary makes its own hormones under control of releasing factors.

questions.stem: How does ADH increase water reabsorption in the collecting ducts?
options: By making the loop of Henle longer
By raising the glomerular filtration rate
By pumping sodium out of the duct
By adding aquaporins to the membrane
questions.explanation: ADH signaling moves vesicles carrying water channels (aquaporins) into the membrane of collecting duct cells, so water can follow the osmotic gradient into the salty medulla.

questions.stem: The results for Patient 2 are best explained by:
options: kidneys that do not respond to ADH
a medulla that is too salty
a pituitary that makes no ADH at all
questions.explanation: Patient 2's urine stayed dilute even after desmopressin, so the hormone was supplied but had no effect, which points to the kidney. Patient 1 concentrated urine once given the drug, so that patient lacks ADH.

questions.stem: During water deprivation, what most directly stimulated the patients' thirst?
options: High levels of ADH in blood
questions.explanation: As both patients kept losing water in urine, plasma sodium and osmolality rose, and hypothalamic osmoreceptors drive thirst. Their urine stayed dilute, so it was not rising urine osmolality.

questions.stem: Which hormone acts on the distal nephron to increase sodium reabsorption, raising blood volume?
questions.explanation: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal tubule and collecting duct; water follows the sodium. Calcitonin lowers blood calcium.

questions.stem: The loops of Henle are essential for the healthy volunteer's urine of 900 mOsm/kg because they:
options: pump water into the collecting duct
questions.explanation: Countercurrent multiplication by the loops builds a very salty medullary interstitium, and only that gradient lets water leave the collecting duct when ADH opens its channels.

questions.stem: Phosphofructokinase-1 is inhibited by ATP and activated by AMP. When a muscle cell's AMP level rises during hard exercise, glycolysis will:
questions.explanation: A high AMP level signals low energy, and AMP activates phosphofructokinase-1, the main control point of glycolysis, so flux through the pathway increases to make more ATP.

questions.stem: A recessive trait appears in 1 of every 400 people in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. About what percent of people are carriers?
questions.explanation: q² = 1/400, so q = 0.05 and p = 0.95, and carriers are 2pq = 2 x 0.95 x 0.05 = 0.095, or 9.5%. 5% is the recessive allele frequency, not the carrier frequency.

questions.stem: One pair of homologous chromosomes fails to separate in meiosis I in a primary spermatocyte, and meiosis II is normal. How many of the four resulting sperm have an abnormal chromosome number?
questions.explanation: If homologs fail to separate in meiosis I, one secondary cell gets both and the other none, so all four products are aneuploid (two with an extra chromosome, two missing one). Nondisjunction in meiosis II affects only two.

questions.stem: How many acetyl-CoA molecules does the complete beta-oxidation of one palmitate (16 carbons) produce?
questions.explanation: Each acetyl-CoA carries two carbons, so 16 carbons give 8. It takes 7 rounds, because the last round splits a four-carbon unit into two acetyl-CoA.

questions.stem: A plasmid passes from one bacterium to another through a pilus that joins the two cells. This process is called:
questions.explanation: Conjugation is DNA transfer by direct contact. Transformation is uptake of free DNA from the surroundings, and transduction is transfer by a bacteriophage.

questions.stem: Which molecule crosses a pure phospholipid bilayer most readily by simple diffusion?
questions.explanation: Small nonpolar molecules such as O2 dissolve in the hydrophobic core and diffuse straight through. Glucose, ions and charged amino acids need transport proteins.

questions.stem: Deoxygenated blood returning from the body first enters which chamber of the heart?
questions.explanation: The venae cavae empty into the right atrium, then blood passes to the right ventricle and the lungs. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins.

questions.stem: The rising phase of a neuron's action potential is caused mainly by:
options: potassium flowing out through leak channels
sodium flowing in through voltage-gated channels
chloride flowing in through ligand-gated channels
questions.explanation: Once threshold is reached, voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na⁺ rushes in, driving the membrane positive. Potassium leaving through voltage-gated channels then repolarizes it.

questions.stem: The design of the study, with testing after recovery sleep, is best suited to show that sleep helps which memory process?
questions.explanation: Both groups learned while rested and were tested while rested, so the difference must come from what happened between, when new memories are stabilized. Encoding happened before the groups were split.

questions.stem: What is the independent variable in the main study?
options: The number of word pairs learned
The percentage of word pairs recalled at test
questions.explanation: The researchers manipulated whether students slept or stayed awake; recall is the dependent variable. Slow-wave sleep was measured, not assigned.

questions.stem: The link between slow-wave sleep and recall best supports which conclusion?
options: Slow-wave sleep directly causes better recall
Deep sleep is associated with better recall
REM sleep is unrelated to memory
questions.explanation: Time in slow-wave sleep was measured, not manipulated, so the finding is a correlation and cannot by itself show cause. Nothing in the study measured REM sleep.

questions.stem: The task in which students pressed a key for a rare letter in a stream of common ones mainly measured:
questions.explanation: Watching a stream for rare targets tests vigilance, the ability to keep attention on one task over time. The task did not require doing two things at once.

questions.stem: Staying awake all night is a physical stressor. Which hormone, released by the adrenal cortex under control of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, would most likely rise?
questions.explanation: Stress activates the HPA axis: CRH from the hypothalamus, ACTH from the pituitary, then cortisol from the adrenal cortex. Melatonin comes from the pineal gland and tracks darkness.

questions.stem: Caffeine helped some students stay awake. It reduces sleepiness mainly by:
questions.explanation: Adenosine builds up during waking and promotes sleep pressure; caffeine blocks its receptors. Stimulating GABA receptors would sedate rather than alert.

questions.stem: The drop in conformity when answers were written privately suggests that most conformity in these studies reflected:
questions.explanation: People conformed mainly when the group could hear them, and they said they did not want to seem odd, which is the wish to be accepted, or normative influence. Informational influence would persist in private, since it changes what people believe.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what most reduced conformity?
options: Answering aloud rather than in private writing
One other person giving the correct answer
Adding more people to the group
questions.explanation: A single ally who gave the correct answer cut conformity to about 6%. Adding people beyond three changed little, and answering aloud raised conformity.

questions.stem: Which result best shows that the effect of group size on conformity has a limit?
options: Drop when answers were given privately
Rise from one to three others
questions.explanation: Conformity rose up to three others and then leveled off, so adding people stopped making a difference. The rise alone shows an effect but not its limit.

questions.stem: The observers' explanations of the conforming participants best illustrate:
questions.explanation: Observers explained behavior by personality (weak-willed) and overlooked the strong situational pressure, which is the fundamental attribution error. The self-serving bias concerns explanations of one's own outcomes.

questions.stem: Participants who gave the wrong answer aloud so as not to seem odd to the others, yet answered correctly in private, were most clearly engaged in:
questions.explanation: Adjusting public behavior to control how others see you is impression management, part of self-presentation. Dissonance is the discomfort of holding conflicting beliefs or acts.

questions.stem: The highway and waste station along Riverside's edge best illustrate which concept?
questions.explanation: Environmental justice concerns how health risks such as pollution fall unequally on poorer and minority neighborhoods. Cultural capital refers to knowledge and tastes that confer advantage.

questions.stem: Banks once refusing to lend in Riverside is an example of:
questions.explanation: Unequal treatment built into the practices of organizations such as banks is institutional discrimination, and its effects can last after the policy ends. It does not depend on any one person's prejudice.

questions.stem: The health department's report is most consistent with which sociological perspective?
questions.explanation: Conflict theory explains outcomes through unequal power and resources between groups, as in the report's focus on the city's history of lending and land use. Rational choice theory would stress individual decisions, which the report says cannot explain the gap alone.
